CASE PUD 2026-000031 ENTRY NO. 124 FILED IN OCC COURT CLERK'S OFFICE ON 08/31/2026 - PAGE 1 OF 4




           BEFORE THE CORPORATION COMMISSION OF THE STATE OF OKLAHOMA

          IN THE MATTER OF THE APPLICATION OF                         )
          OKLAHOMA GAS AND ELECTRIC COMPANY                           ) Case No. PUD2026-000031
          FOR COMMISSION APPROVAL OF ELECTRIC                         )
          SERVICE AGREEMENTS AND PREAPPROVAL                          )
          OF CAPACITY PURCHASE AGREEMENTS                             )
          PURSUANT TO 17 O.S. § 286(C)                                )



                   Redacted Confidential Testimony Summary of Matthew J. Schuermann

         Direct Testimony

                 In his Direct Testimony, Matthew J. Schuermann first provided his educational
         qualifications and employment history. He explained the purpose of his testimony is to support
         the pre-approval of capacity resources that have been selected by the Company to meet the
         resource adequacy needs as shown in its 2024 and 2025 Integrated Resource Plans. Specifically,
         he testified that OG&E is requesting pre-approval for two Capacity Purchase Agreements, which
         are associated with the special contracts also being presented in this case.

                 Mr. Schuermann testified that the two generating resources associated with the Capacity
         Purchase Agreements are the Rush Springs facility, a solar generation project under construction
         with a nameplate rating of 200MW and an expected in-service date during the spring of 2027, and
         the High Spring facility, also a solar generation project under construction with a nameplate rating
         of 400MW and an expected in-service date during the spring of 2028. He stated that the CPAs, in
         combination, would provide approximately 360MW of accredited capacity during the summer
         resource adequacy periods and approximately 120MW of accredited capacity during the winter
         resource adequacy periods. He further noted that although this addition does not fully address the
         Company’s projected capacity shortfall over the coming years, it does represent an important
         progression towards meeting and supporting the Company’s capacity requirements.

                 Mr. Schuermann explained that the negotiations for providing electric service to certain
         Google sites have been in process for over a year, and that Google first introduced the topic related
         to their ability to offer capacity resources in January of 2025. He testified that Google does not
         own the generation facilities but has a contract to acquire
                   from both Rush Springs and High Spring, which provides Google with the rights to sell
         the capacity to another party. He described each CPA as providing both summer and winter
         capacity for a term of 15 years, with the Rush Springs CPA beginning with the 2027 summer
         period and the High Spring CPA beginning with the 2028 summer period. He stated that the
         Company will only pay for the amount of capacity that is actually scheduled and received during
         the periods, with the specific amount of capacity varying depending on the accreditation assigned
         by the Southwest Power Pool. He testified that the cost for each CPA is fixed over the 15-year
         term at

                 Mr. Schuermann then testified regarding the competitiveness of the CPA pricing, stating
         that compared to other bids offered into the Company’s 2024 All Source RFP, the price for both
         CPAs is roughly 26% lower than the lowest-cost bid initially offered, although that bid was later
         withdrawn, and approximately 58% lower when compared to the least-cost CPA the Company
         ultimately executed through the RFP. He explained that the CPAs become effective only once the
         Conditions to Effectiveness under the Energy Service Agreements are satisfied or waived, and that
         if those conditions are not met by the ESA long-stop date, either party may terminate the CPAs
         with no further liability. He described several protections built into the contracts, including that
         Google must deliver the greater of the accredited capacity assigned by SPP or the capacity it would
         have received if fully available, protecting OG&E from capacity reductions caused by delays,
         derates, or operational issues. He further stated that if Google fails to deliver the required capacity,
         it must pay the net cost difference between the contracted rate and the cost of replacement capacity,
         any regulatory penalties arising from the failure, and its proportional share of any SPP Deficiency
         Payments, and that failures by project owners are treated as failures by Google such that force
         majeure cannot be used to avoid liability.

                 Mr. Schuermann testified that the CPAs provide significant benefits, including a material
         quantity of capacity at the lowest cost available to the Company, alternate facilities to supply the
         needed capacity in the event that either the Rush Springs or High Spring facilities are not available,
         and a contract structure that allows OG&E to receive needed capacity without taking on the energy
         market pricing risk of a Power Purchase Agreement that includes both the purchase of capacity
         and energy. He concluded by recommending the Commission grant pre-approval of the CPAs,
         stating that these projects are priced below market and that based on his experience, he believes
         these projects will provide significant value to customers.

         Rebuttal Testimony

                  In his Rebuttal Testimony, Mr. Schuermann explains the overall purpose of his testimony
         is to respond to arguments raised in Responsive Testimony regarding the analysis and evaluation
         of the two Capacity Purchase Agreements that OG&E is seeking approval of in this case.
         Specifically, he addresses questions regarding the Company’s consideration of reasonable
         alternatives, the use of prior Request for Proposal information as a market benchmark, and the
         importance of evaluating all available resource opportunities to secure the lowest-cost and best-
         value resources for customers.

                 Mr. Schuermann testified that he disagrees with PUD witness Givens’ recommendation
         that the Commission should set an intentionally high bar to discourage utilities from evading RFP
         requirements. He stated that there is no basis for this recommendation and rejected the insinuation
         that OG&E may try to evade RFP requirements. He explained that while OG&E is very supportive
         of the RFP process and will continue to utilize it, sometimes there are opportunities that arise
         outside of an RFP process that are the best options for customers. He testified that resource
         opportunities become known to the Company through a variety of channels, including bilateral
         discussions with developers, interactions with customers, market outreach, industry conferences,
         existing commercial relationships, unsolicited proposals, and ongoing procurement activities. He
         noted that in this case, the opportunity to secure this capacity arose during negotiations associated
         with Google’s electric service requirements. He stated that OG&E’s obligation is to develop the

         lowest reasonable cost portfolio that reliably serves customers, and that limiting evaluation only
         to resources received through a particular solicitation could cause the Company to overlook
         opportunities that provide significant value to customers. He further testified that it would be
         irresponsible and imprudent for OG&E to ignore potentially favorable opportunities simply
         because they originated outside of a formal solicitation.

                 Mr. Schuermann then testified regarding what would have happened if OG&E had not
         contracted for these CPAs and waited for a future RFP. He stated that the Company would likely
         have lost access to this opportunity because the CPAs were offered as part of the broader
         commercial arrangement associated with Google’s facilities and are contingent upon the related
         agreements. He noted that these resources appear to be a unique opportunity that likely would not
         be available in a future RFP. He further explained that since execution of these agreements, the
         Company has continued to evaluate market alternatives through more recent procurement efforts,
         and that OG&E did not receive comparable offers for these early delivery years in either the
         ongoing Bridge Capacity RFP or the current All Source RFP, and the costs of resources available
         through those solicitations have been higher than the pricing for these CPAs. He also testified that
         he generally agrees with Mr. Mossburg’s conclusions that the CPAs feature reasonable protections
         for ratepayers, are priced substantially below comparable market alternatives, and represent a
         unique opportunity because they are linked to the ESA transaction.

                 Mr. Schuermann testified that he disagrees with PUD witness Givens’ assertion that a
         comparison of reasonable alternatives was impossible in this case. He noted that Mr. Givens
         acknowledged the pricing under the CPAs is very favorable. He explained that OG&E did perform
         a comparison of reasonable alternatives, as detailed in his Direct Testimony along with OG&E
         witness Shoop, and that RFPs are not the only way to compare reasonable alternatives. He testified
         that OG&E compared the CPAs to other bids offered into the Company’s 2024 All Source RFP, as
         well as to other bilateral opportunities and market transactions that were available. He stated that
         OG&E’s evaluation concluded that the price of the CPAs was lower than any other available
         capacity and therefore favorable as compared to reasonable alternatives. Specifically, he testified
         that the CPA pricing was 26 percent lower than the lowest cost bid initially offered into the 2024
         All Source RFP, and approximately 58 percent lower than the least cost CPA and the highest ranked
         project OG&E ultimately executed through the RFP.

                 Mr. Schuermann concluded by testifying that OG&E exercised reasonable business
         judgment in evaluating and pursuing a unique opportunity that addressed an established capacity
         need and compared favorably to available alternatives. He noted that no witness in this case
         identified any better options for capacity than the CPAs requested for approval.
